title: Interviewing Stakeholders and Mapping Incentives
intro: Interview for raw material, not requirements. Then pitch on what each person is rewarded for.

learn.title: Interview for raw material
learn.text:
Don’t ask stakeholders for requirements. You will get solutions, and the first one they thought of.

Ask for raw material across three areas: the **domain**, the **audience**, and the **constraints** — technical, operational and political.

The political constraints decide more than people admit.

try.q: What should you ask stakeholders for?
options: Raw material: purpose, audience, constraints
A complete list of requirements to build
A prioritised backlog of features to ship
A signed-off design brief to work from
try.explain: Requirements arrive as solutions. Raw material lets you find the problem yourself.

learn.title: Questions that work
learn.text:
• “Describe the purpose of this project in your own words.”
• “What is the most important thing to get right?”
• “If you could ask users one question, what would it be?”
• “How will you judge whether this succeeded?”
• Question the labels: “Why do we call them power users?”

Close with **“What did I miss?”**

try.q: Which question should close the interview?
options: “What did I miss?”
“Are we done?”
“Do you approve this plan?”
“When can I have the requirements?”
try.explain: It invites the one thing they didn’t think to say until the end.

learn.title: Map incentives before you pitch
learn.text:
Write down what each person is rewarded for. Typical patterns: product — short-term lift in a headline metric; engineering — uptime and speed; marketing — brand health; support — fewer tickets.

Pitch on a measure the decider cares about. If nothing lines up, **ask what would matter, find a better-aligned stakeholder, or shelve the idea for now.**

try.q: A support lead doubts a usability finding. Which framing helps most?
options: How the fix cuts support tickets
How it improves learnability scores
How it lines up with usability heuristics
How many sessions showed the problem
try.explain: It speaks to what the support lead is rewarded for.

test.q: Which three areas should a stakeholder interview cover?
options: Domain, audience and constraints
Budget, timeline and scope of work
Goals, tasks and the screens involved
Features, priorities and delivery risks
test.explain: These give you raw material to find the problem, rather than a list of solutions.

test.q: Why ask “Why do we call them power users?”
options: To test labels the team takes for granted
To find out exactly who the power users are
To get a clean definition for the glossary
To move the conversation on to personas
test.explain: Labels hide assumptions. Asking what a word means often reveals the assumption behind it.

test.q: Which incentive is typical for engineering?
options: Uptime and delivery speed
Short-term lift in a headline metric
Brand health
Fewer support tickets
test.explain: Engineering is usually rewarded for stable, on-time delivery, so frame the work in those terms.

test.q: What can you do if no stakeholder’s incentives line up with your idea?
options: Ask what matters, find an ally, or shelve it
Present the same evidence more often to them
Escalate the issue to the most senior person
Reframe the findings so they read as requirements
test.explain: More evidence on a metric the decider doesn’t care about doesn’t help. Change the audience or the pitch.

test.q: Why does a pitch fail when it uses the wrong metric?
options: The decider isn’t rewarded for that measure
The supporting data is usually out of date
Evidence never changes anyone’s mind at all
The presentation is almost always too long
test.explain: People act on what they are rewarded for. A finding that doesn’t touch it is easy to set aside.
